title: GST/HST for Small Businesses
subtitle: Know when to register, what to charge, and what to send

blocks.text: GST/HST isn’t just an extra percentage added to an invoice. It’s a system built on four linked decisions: whether the business must register, whether a sale is taxable, which rate applies and how much net tax you report and send in.

Make those decisions in the right order, and GST/HST becomes routine. Try to rebuild them from memory after the sale, and an invoice can turn into a small detective novel with no satisfying final chapter.

This is general Canadian education, not personal tax, accounting, legal or business advice. GST/HST, QST and provincial sales tax rules change, and they depend on what you sell, to whom, where and how your business is set up. Check anything time-sensitive with the CRA, Revenu Québec where it applies, or a qualified professional. Each section here answers one question in order: must I register, is the sale taxable, which rate applies, what can I claim back, and when do I file and pay. The order matters. Tax websites already enjoy sending people back to earlier screens.

items.title: “GST/HST collected is extra profit.”
items.text: Collected tax belongs in a tax-payable record, not the owner’s spending plan. Sales and tax can arrive in the same customer payment while doing completely different jobs.

blocks.text: Handle sales tax with confidence, and never get caught charging too little or too late.
blocks.detail: Making four decisions in the right order keeps your prices honest, your claims safe and your cash where it belongs.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows the two ways to cross the $30,000 line.

sections.title: Separate Sales Tax From Business Income

blocks.text: GST is a federal sales tax charged at each step of the sale chain. Some provinces combine their own sales tax with GST and call it HST. The rate you charge depends on the place-of-supply rules and the type of sale, not just where the seller is.

For a registered business, GST/HST collected from customers isn’t normal income. The business holds that tax in trust and reports it on a GST/HST return. Under the regular method, input tax credits (ITCs) on business purchases can reduce the net amount you send in.

Income tax works differently. It’s based on taxable income after deductions. A business can owe income tax without being registered for GST/HST, and it can file a GST/HST return with little or no profit. Keep the two calculations, and their deadlines, apart.
Put the GST/HST part of every payment into a separate bookkeeping category right away. A separate savings account adds protection. Money with a government name tag has a habit of being needed later.

Most businesses selling taxable goods or services in Canada must register once they stop being a small supplier. Under the general rule, the line is $30,000 of taxable sales worldwide, including zero-rated sales, before expenses. Sales by related businesses may need to be added in.
You can cross the line in two different ways.

items.title: ONE CALENDAR QUARTER
items.text: Pass $30,000 in a single quarter, and you stop being a small supplier with the sale that pushed you over. You must register within 29 days, and you must charge GST/HST on that same sale. That’s why a large contract deserves a registration check before the invoice goes out.

items.title: FOUR CONSECUTIVE CALENDAR QUARTERS
items.text: Pass $30,000 over four quarters in a row, without crossing it in any single one, and the timing is different. You stop being a small supplier at the end of the month after that four-quarter period, and must register within 29 days. Confirm the exact dates with the CRA’s current guidance.

blocks.text: Track the running total every month. The test uses taxable sales before expenses, not profit. A business with thin margins can still cross the line.

items.title: “I only test the $30,000 threshold at year-end.”
items.text: One test looks at a single calendar quarter. The other looks at four quarters in a row. December isn’t the only month with a calculator.

blocks.text: Special registration rules

Some activities have their own rules. Taxi and commercial ride-sharing drivers must register from their first sale, even below $30,000. Non-residents, charities, public bodies, real estate sales, digital businesses and some other activities may have their own rules too.
The $30,000 limit applies to all of a person’s taxable sales together, not separately to each brand, marketplace or side business. Three small sales channels don’t create three separate limits.
Voluntary registration

A small supplier can usually register by choice. It lets you claim ITCs on business purchases, but it also brings duties: charging and collecting tax, filing returns, keeping records and generally staying registered for at least a year. Weigh your customers, expected purchases, prices and paperwork before you register just because an online form had a friendly green button.

sections.title: Classify the Sale Before Choosing a Rate

blocks.text: Registering doesn’t mean every sale is taxed the same way. Sort each sale into a category first.

items.title: TAXABLE SUPPLIES
items.text: Most goods and services sold in business are taxable. A registered business charges GST/HST at the right rate and may claim ITCs on the costs of that work.

items.title: ZERO-RATED SUPPLIES
items.text: Taxed at zero percent. The seller doesn’t collect GST/HST but can usually still claim ITCs on the costs of making the sale. Basic groceries, prescription drugs, some medical devices and exports can qualify when the rules are met.

items.title: EXEMPT SUPPLIES
items.text: No GST/HST is charged, and unlike zero-rated sales, costs used to make exempt sales generally can’t be claimed as ITCs. Examples can include many health, education, child care, residential rent and financial services. Each has its own conditions.

blocks.text: An invoice can show no tax for both zero-rated and exempt sales, but the business result isn’t the same. Whether you can claim ITCs is one big difference.

items.title: “No tax on the invoice means the sale is exempt.”
items.text: A sale can be zero-rated, exempt, outside the GST/HST system or made by someone who isn’t registered. An empty tax line doesn’t explain why it’s empty.

blocks.text: Write the tax category beside every product or service on your price list. Do the research once, note where you found the answer and review it when your offer changes. Guessing at checkout is a poor customer-service feature.
Use place-of-supply rules

The rate can depend on where the sale is considered made. Goods, services, digital products and real estate each follow different rules, so a seller in Alberta can make a sale subject to HST in another province. A customer’s billing address often matters, but it isn’t the whole answer. Use the CRA’s place-of-supply guidance and keep the customer details you used to choose the rate.

sections.title: Elena Catches the Threshold Before the Invoice

blocks.text: Elena catches the line before the invoice
paragraphs: Elena ran a small workplace-training business from her home in Dartmouth. She checked her sales once a year, at tax time, and had never come close to $30,000 in a quarter.

Then a national client asked her to run a large training project, $26,000 of work, all to be delivered in one quarter. She already had $7,000 of other sales booked for those same three months. She was thrilled, and she started drafting the usual invoice with no HST.

Halfway through, something nagged at her. A friend in bookkeeping had once mentioned a quarterly limit. She could send the invoice now and sort out tax later, or she could stop and check. She opened a spreadsheet and added up the quarter: $33,000. The project would push her over the line.

She called an accountant that afternoon. He confirmed she had to register within 29 days and charge HST on the sale that crossed $30,000. Elena registered, added her GST/HST number to a new invoice template and checked that 14% HST applied, since her client would receive the training in Nova Scotia. She also opened a separate account for the tax she would collect.

Then she called the client before sending anything. She explained that her price hadn’t changed, but HST would now appear on its own line. The client’s finance team didn’t blink. As a registered business, they would claim the HST back.

At filing time, Elena’s sales, the tax she collected and her claims for HST paid on her laptop and training materials all matched the return. She now checks her running total on the first of every month, not once a year.

blocks.text: A two-minute check before a big invoice can save you months of cleanup.
blocks.detail: Watching your quarterly total lets you register on time, charge correctly and keep your clients’ trust.
blocks.extra: Section 06 shows what every invoice and claim needs.

sections.title: Build Invoices and ITCs From Evidence

blocks.text: A registered business’s invoices should clearly support the tax charged. Depending on the amount, they may need the seller’s name, invoice date, total, GST/HST charged (or a note that it’s included), GST/HST number, buyer’s name, payment terms and a description of what was sold.

Use an invoice template that saves the customer’s location, sale date, subtotal, rate, tax, total and payment status. Number invoices in order. If one needs fixing, keep the original and issue a credit note or a replacement, instead of quietly editing it.
Input tax credits

An ITC lets a registered business recover GST/HST paid on purchases used in its business, but only with the right paperwork from a registered supplier. Personal costs, costs of exempt sales and amounts without proof don’t become ITCs just because they went on a business credit card. Claim them within four years.
What a receipt must show to claim an ITC

items.title: Under $100
items.text: Basics — the seller’s name, the date and the total.

items.title: $100 to $499.99
items.text: Add the tax — the GST/HST amount and the seller’s GST/HST number.

items.title: $500 or more
items.text: Add the details — your name, a description of the purchase and the payment terms.

blocks.text: For purchases used partly for personal reasons, claim only the business share. Equipment has its own ITC rules, and meals and entertainment, cars, home offices and changes in use can all have limits or special math.

items.title: “Any receipt showing GST/HST supports an ITC.”
items.text: You still have to meet the rules and hold the right paperwork. A tax amount printed on paper is a starting point, not a permission slip.

blocks.text: Check a supplier’s GST/HST number when an invoice looks unusual or the claim is large. The CRA has an online registry for it. ITCs shouldn’t rely on a number assembled with creative punctuation.

items.title: REGULAR METHOD
items.text: Start with the GST/HST you charged, then subtract the ITCs you can support. This is the standard, itemized way.

items.title: QUICK METHOD
items.text: Eligible businesses with $400,000 or less in taxable sales send in a set percentage of their sales instead, and claim far fewer ITCs, since those costs are built into the rate. It’s a formal choice, not a shortcut picked after the return is done. Compare both with a professional first, since less math doesn’t always mean less tax.

sections.title: File the Return, Even When the Period Was Quiet

blocks.text: The CRA assigns a reporting period: usually yearly, quarterly or monthly. Deadlines depend on that period and your situation. A person filing yearly with business income may even have a payment date before the filing date. Use the due dates in your CRA business account or the official filing information.

Most registered businesses must file online for reporting periods starting in 2024 or later, with a few exceptions. You can use your CRA business account or GST/HST NETFILE. Quebec businesses generally file GST and QST through Revenu Québec.
File every required return, including a nil return when you owe nothing. You stay registered until the account is formally closed. Ignoring it doesn’t make the filing calendar lose interest.

Match three totals before you file: taxable sales, GST/HST charged and ITCs you can support. Then compare the result with your tax-payable account. A return should sum up your books, not introduce itself to them.
Charged versus collected

Usually, the invoice date decides when tax must be reported, even if the customer hasn’t paid yet. A business can owe tax before the cash arrives. Deposits, bad debts, credit notes and billing in instalments can need special handling. Protect your cash flow by stating payment terms, following up on unpaid invoices and moving collected tax out of operating money. GST/HST won’t wait politely beside an overdue invoice.
Correct errors openly

Charged the wrong rate, missed a registration date, claimed an ITC without proof or filed the wrong amount? Don’t quietly change old records. Keep the paper trail and use the CRA’s process to fix it: an adjustment, a voluntary disclosure or an objection, as the case may be. Get advice when the amount or time period is large.

sections.title: What Changes by Province or Territory

blocks.text: HST applies in Ontario and the Atlantic provinces. Everywhere else, GST applies, and British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec run their own provincial sales taxes alongside it. Alberta and the territories have no general provincial sales tax.

Quebec generally runs both GST and QST for businesses located there. QST registration, invoices, refunds of tax paid, reporting and place-of-supply rules each need a Quebec-specific check. A federal GST/HST account doesn’t cover every QST duty.

Provincial sales taxes aren’t copies of GST/HST. Registration limits, what’s taxed, exemptions, marketplace rules and filing systems all differ. If you sell goods, software, lodging or services across Canada, map each province or territory where customers receive what you sell. For each regular kind of sale, note the seller’s location, the customer’s location, the delivery location, the type of sale and the tax charged. That small file beats a colour-coded map with no rules behind it.
Key takeaway

GST/HST works best as a set of steps: track the $30,000 line before you invoice, sort each sale, apply the right place-of-supply rule, collect and record the tax separately, claim only ITCs you can support and file every return on time. The best protection isn’t memorizing every rate. It’s knowing which fact to check before the sale.

Build a one-page GST/HST control sheet: registration date, reporting period, filing and payment deadlines, sales-tax codes, the account for collected tax, invoice template version, ITC paperwork checklist and who reviews it. Update it whenever the business adds a new product, province, platform or large contract.

items.title: Why isn't GST/HST collected ordinary business revenue?
items.detail: A registered business holds collected GST/HST in trust, then reports it and sends in the net amount on its return.

items.title: What two time periods do the general small-supplier threshold tests use?
items.detail: A single calendar quarter, and four calendar quarters in a row.

items.title: What's one important difference between zero-rated and exempt supplies?
items.detail: You can generally claim ITCs on costs linked to zero-rated sales, but not on costs used to make exempt sales.

items.title: Why might a business in one province need to charge another province's rate?
items.detail: Place-of-supply rules can base the rate on where the sale is considered made or delivered, not just where the seller is.

items.title: Why might GST/HST be payable before the customer pays the invoice?
items.detail: Usually, tax becomes reportable based on the invoice date, even when the customer hasn’t paid yet.

sections.title: Your Action: Complete a GST/HST Registration Decision Record

blocks.text: Don’t register or change an invoice for this exercise. Just collect the facts first. This is preparation, not a filing.
This is fact-finding, not a filing. The goal is to stop an invoice going out on an untested tax guess. Leave account numbers and filed returns out of this form.

items.title: Exempt supply
items.text: A sale with no GST/HST, where the related costs generally can’t be claimed as ITCs.

items.title: GST/HST registrant
items.text: A person or business registered, or required to register, for a GST/HST account.

items.title: Input tax credit (ITC)
items.text: A claim that lets a registered business recover GST/HST paid on purchases used in its business.

items.title: Place of supply
items.text: The legal location used to decide whether GST/HST applies, and at what rate.

items.title: Quick Method
items.text: An optional way to work out GST/HST, using set rates for eligible small businesses and fewer ITC claims.

items.title: Reporting period
items.text: The monthly, quarterly or yearly period one GST/HST return covers.

items.title: Small supplier
items.text: A business whose taxable sales stay within the $30,000 tests and that isn’t required to register under a special rule.

items.title: Taxable supply
items.text: A business sale that GST/HST applies to, including a zero-rated sale.

items.title: Zero-rated supply
items.text: A taxable sale taxed at zero percent, where the related costs can usually be claimed as ITCs.

quiz.question: True or False: “GST/HST collected is extra profit.”

questions: What products or services does your business sell?
Is each one taxable, zero-rated, exempt, or does it need review?
What were your taxable sales this quarter and over the last four quarters?
Do any special rules apply, such as ride-sharing, a related business or sales from outside Canada?
Where do your customers receive what you sell?
Who will confirm your registration decision, and by when?
